course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

topic.title: Developing an American Identity
topic.summary: How Americans expressed a national identity after the Revolution in language, literature, art, and architecture, while regional differences continued.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes how Noah Webster's spelling book and dictionary reflected a new national culture?
choices: They taught American children to use British spelling and grammar in order to preserve ties with Britain
They promoted a standard American form of English and taught republican values and love of country
They translated the Constitution into the languages of the immigrant groups living in the new states
They described the geography and natural history of the western territories for settlers moving west
questions.explanation: Webster wanted American schools to teach an American form of English and to instill civic virtue.
choiceExplanations: Webster promoted American usage.
Webster wanted American schools to teach an American form of English and to instill civic virtue.
Webster's books were aimed at American English and education.
Webster's works concerned language and education.
questions.distinguisher: The British-spelling choice is close because the spelling book was about spelling, but its purpose was to promote an American standard.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The neoclassical style in American architecture drew on
choices: Gothic cathedrals, which Americans associated with the Church of England and the English monarchy
Spanish mission buildings, which Americans admired because of the missions in California and Florida
Greek and Roman models, which Americans associated with republican government
Native American structures, which Americans adopted to show their separation from European traditions
questions.explanation: Thomas Jefferson's designs for the Virginia state capitol and Monticello used classical forms to express the ideals of the republic.
choiceExplanations: Neoclassical style did not draw on Gothic cathedrals.
Neoclassical style drew on classical models.
Thomas Jefferson's designs for the Virginia state capitol and Monticello used classical forms to express the ideals of the republic.
Neoclassical style drew on Greek and Roman forms.
questions.distinguisher: The Gothic choice is close because it was an important European style, but American leaders chose classical models for a republic.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why writers and artists in the early republic tried to create a distinctly American culture?
choices: Independence created a need for a national identity that matched the new republic
The Constitution required the federal government to sponsor art and literature that praised the republic
Britain had banned the sale of British books and paintings in the United States after the Revolution
Most Americans had no schools or churches, so culture had to be created entirely from nothing
questions.explanation: Leaders believed that a republic needed a shared culture, and they wished to show that America had its own character.
choiceExplanations: Leaders believed that a republic needed a shared culture, and they wished to show that America had its own character.
The Constitution did not require government sponsorship of culture.
Britain did not ban the sale of its books in the United States.
Americans had schools, churches, and cultural traditions inherited from the colonial period.
questions.distinguisher: The Constitution choice is close because the new government mattered to culture, but the Constitution did not require art.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Royall Tyler's play The Contrast (1787) is an example of a work that
choices: praised British customs and urged Americans to follow the fashions of London
described the rules of the Constitutional Convention and the compromises that delegates reached
argued for an end to slavery by describing the suffering of enslaved people on southern plantations
contrasted American simplicity with European manners to express national identity
questions.explanation: Writers in the early republic used American themes and characters to build a national literature.
choiceExplanations: The play praised American qualities over European manners.
The play was a comedy and not a record of the Convention.
The play was not mainly about slavery.
Writers in the early republic used American themes and characters to build a national literature.
questions.distinguisher: The British-customs choice is close because the play contained a British-style character, but it favored American simplicity.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following represented a change in the relationship between government and religion after the Revolution?
choices: Every state established the Church of England as its official church after the Treaty of Paris
Several states ended official support for churches, and Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom separated church and state
Congress required every citizen to belong to a church in order to vote in federal elections
The Constitution made the Congregational Church the official church of the United States
questions.explanation: The Revolution encouraged ideas of religious liberty, and some states ended the official support that churches had received in the colonial period.
choiceExplanations: Several states ended official support for churches.
The Revolution encouraged ideas of religious liberty, and some states ended the official support that churches had received in the colonial period.
Congress had no such requirement.
The Constitution did not establish a national church.
questions.distinguisher: The Church of England choice is close because it was established in some colonies, but the Revolution weakened it.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a difference between the regions of the early republic?
choices: The South had most of the nation's cities and factories, while New England depended on plantations
The backcountry had the oldest cities in the nation, while the coastal regions were mostly forest
New England and the Middle Atlantic depended on towns, commerce, and small farms, while the South depended on plantations and slavery
New England depended on slavery for its main exports, while the South relied on free wage labor
questions.explanation: Regional economies and societies remained different even as a national culture was developing.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the economic patterns of the two regions.
The coastal regions had the oldest cities.
Regional economies and societies remained different even as a national culture was developing.
The South depended on slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed-economy choice is close because it uses the same regions, but it swaps their economic patterns.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role of portraits and history paintings by artists such as Gilbert Stuart and John Trumbull?
choices: They honored Revolutionary leaders and events and helped create a shared national memory
They criticized the Constitution and called for a return to the Articles of Confederation
They depicted the daily lives of enslaved workers and of poor farmers on the frontier
They encouraged colonists to remain loyal to the king by showing the glory of the British Empire
questions.explanation: Art about the founders and the Revolution helped Americans see themselves as a nation with a common past.
choiceExplanations: Art about the founders and the Revolution helped Americans see themselves as a nation with a common past.
These works honored the leaders and events of the Revolution.
These artists mostly portrayed political leaders and public events.
These works came after independence and honored the new nation.
questions.distinguisher: The criticism choice is close because artists could disagree with leaders, but these works were commemorative.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why there was new attention to education, including the education of girls, in the early republic?
choices: The Constitution required every state to open public schools and to educate all children
British schools were closed after the war, and Americans had to replace them quickly with new ones
Women demanded the right to vote, and the states agreed to educate them to prepare them for elections
Republican government depended on informed citizens, and mothers were expected to teach civic virtue
questions.explanation: Leaders believed that a republic needed educated, virtuous citizens, which gave education a civic purpose.
choiceExplanations: The Constitution did not require public schools.
Americans educated their children before and after the war.
Most women could not vote in the early republic.
Leaders believed that a republic needed educated, virtuous citizens, which gave education a civic purpose.
questions.distinguisher: The Constitution choice is close because the nation was new, but education remained a matter for the states and families.
